I recall one incident when a young saxophonist who was playing in your orchestra on one of the tours to Japan came to you and asked you about fingering, and he said, “When do you use this particular key?” or whatever. And you said, “I never use that key.” And then he said, “Really?” And then you showed him something else, and then he went away, and you told me, “Oh, wait a minute. Go get him back, because I can’t understand how I said that.” [Carter laughs.] “Because there’s no way I could be playing these notes. I do use that key; I just didn’t know I used it.”
I did. I just didn’t know it. That’s right. Well, it becomes automatic, you know.
So the instrument is so much a part of your . . . it almost seems to become a part of your anatomy, I guess, to you.
Well, it becomes that, surely. Yes. It’s just an extension, you know.

So you were never really one of these people that was interested in various ways of attaining a particular note. It seems that you, you know, it just lays naturally to you. You don’t think about the theory behind it. Is that true?
No, indeed not. No. No.

When you finally did start teaching students, and you weren’t really giving them saxophone lessons; I mean, you were discussing music theory on occasion, doing workshops, listening to students play, critiquing their work. But not so much unless they had a particular problem, they would come to you, but you didn’t have a Benny Carter method that you were presenting to them.
No.
But what sort of things do you feel you can impart and do you try to impart when you do get in a classroom situation?

Well, when you say “do,” you mean “did,” because I’m not really doing that anymore. I don’t have the time, and what time that I do have, I devote to performing, you know. I’m slowing down considerably, I guess, as I should do at eighty-five. But I don’t know. There are different things, different problems, and what we’d try to deal with one on one. As a matter of fact, I always had the attitude that there were many things that I could learn. You know, teaching is really a learning experience, and I think we all realize that. Many times a student would have a problem about something and he’d want to know about something, something which I may have known or I may not have known, and I’d say, “Well, gee, that’s an interesting question or a problem. Let’s look it up together,” and I’d pull down one of the many books that I had with me, and we would look it up together. He would realize that I was not really the know-it-all that some teachers are. But I think for the most part that we all realize that we don’t know it all, and we all realize that we can learn much from students.

I think that was brought out at the recent concerts you gave at Rutgers, where you were dealing with a combined . . . professional jazz musicians, some student musicians, symphonic musicians. One of the points they made when I talked to them afterwards, the students, particularly, was that they had never worked with anyone who asked them so many questions about how they wanted to play something. Is that something you do to make people at ease, or to honestly solicit their opinions?

To honestly solicit their opinions and honestly to learn something from them, you know. I think if you give them a part in whatever decisions you make instead of saying, “Now, you’ve got to play it just like this. You’ve got to play it just like that,” well, many times they know and have a feeling for it, because of what it is and how it lays on the instrument, that can make the overall result much more interesting. So I like to enlist their assistance and their ideas.

I’ve noticed at some of the workshops and master classes that you’ve given in recent years that the first activity you have the students engage in is when they play for you. They may jump up and demonstrate tremendous pyrotechnics on whatever instrument they’re playing, and you will stop them and say, “Could you just play a melody?” Or after they’ve finished this dazzling display, you will just ask them to play a melody. Why is that?

Well, I want to see what kind of soul they have, you know. I mean, all it takes to develop a fantastic technique and, as you call them, the master of the pyrotechnics . . . pyro? Not necessarily pyro; well, I guess so. They’re making fire. But it’s just practice, practice, practice. But practice doesn’t necessarily give you feeling or, as we say, from the heart, and I just want to see how they would interpret a melody, what their feeling was toward the music, as well as toward the instrument.
Do you find that melody is being lost? Is that in . . . that you hear today, the appreciation of playing and interpreting a melodic line, with or without embellishment or improvisation?

I don’t know whether it’s being lost, but it’s certainly not being accentuated, you know, because there are many musicians that you hear them display this fantastic technique and dazzling display, they can turn around and play a very nice melody, and you’re surprised, you know.

You just mentioned practicing. I’d like to ask you, you work quite regularly, but there are often large spans of time where you’re either writing something and you’re not playing, or you’re relaxing and not playing. Then you’ll do periods of intensive touring, and then long periods again of inactivity as an actual player. People are always marveling at how you are able to come back after these layoffs seemingly without losing anything. That sort of belies the advice you’re always giving to students about having to practice all the time. What are your practice habits and what sort of things do you do to prepare for an engagement if you haven’t been playing for a while?

Well, I don’t know. I used to practice quite a bit. Now I don’t practice other than when I’m going to do a performance, and then I practice maybe a few days ahead of the performance. I should do it more often, but I just can’t. I can’t bring myself to practice alone. It’s kind of difficult. I’d like to say something about someone. I don’t know who it was that said if I don’t—ooh, what is it? If I don’t play . . . if I don’t practice for a number of days . . . do you know anything about that one?
Not really.

If I don’t practice . . . oh, boy. Oh, if I don’t practice for . . . gee, sorry I don’t remember this correctly, but it’s like if I don’t practice for some length of time, I know it, and if I don’t practice for . . . oh, I don’t know it. I can’t remember it, but it’s first I know it, then you know it, and then everybody knows it, you know. Then the audience knows it, you know. [laughter] So I don’t know about that one. It will come to me immediately when this interview is over.

It reminds me of a line that you once delivered when you decided you were going to play the trumpet in a club, and I believe you said you hadn’t even opened the instrument for six months or so. I think the results were not exactly what you had expected, so you picked up the mic and said, “You pay as I learn,” to the audience. [laughter]
Oh, that was a little while ago.
When you do practice, do you have a regimen that you follow? What do you actually play when you’re by yourself?
No, I’d probably put on a record and play with it. Mostly that rather than scales and exercises.

I heard you once tell a student . . . you got into a discussion about development of jazz and important innovations that you’ve been aware of, and that you had a rather spirited discussion, because you made the statement that you had heard nothing really original, that you found an original contribution, since Charlie Parker. This particular student was a great John Coltrane admirer, and you said, “Well, he was a great technician,” or something, and you even said that you sometimes have practiced by laying transcriptions of his solos.
Of whose solos?
John Coltrane’s.
I said that?
Yes. Never?
I couldn’t possibly have said that.
No?
No. I couldn’t possibly have said that, because it’s not true.
Okay, maybe I misunderstood.
No. I have some Coltrane records that I never play but I have certainly listened to at one time or another, but I probably haven’t played in years. But I’ve never practiced with one of his records.
Well, do you have any of his transcribed solos that you ever looked at?

Yes, I’ve got a lot of them that was done by Andrew White in Washington [D.C.], and I marveled at them, because I don’t know how he did all of this, you know. No, I’ve never tried to play any of that. I’ve looked at it, of course.
The statement that prompted all of this . . .
But now that you’ve mentioned it, maybe next time I practice, I’ll pull them out.
[laughs] Well, it might make an interesting engagement. I want to come to the one after that.
It would make some interesting practice, I’m sure, because that stuff is so intricate and very interesting. Yeah.
You say it’s interesting, but the statement you made to the student, would you stand by that and say that Charlie Parker was the last innovation that you found to be a true departure or a true . . .
For me, yes. For me, yes, Coltrane notwithstanding. I’m sure he made a valuable contribution, but, you know, I think Parker did it. I’m still amazed by it.

While we’re on the subject of Charlie Parker, you did work with him on occasion in recording situations, and I believe you said you did have an opportunity to talk to him and have a conversation with him.
Rather brief, but nonetheless we did, yeah.
And the image you got of him was somewhat different than the one conveyed by various films and some of the jazz literature. Is that true?
I’m not sure about the others, but I know my impression was most favorable, and I would like to have known him much better. And I would like to have heard him in person much oftener, too.

As far as his influence, the cliché has it that nobody that ever played the saxophone could not come to grips with Charlie Parker, and you, of course, had established a style well before Charlie Parker came on the scene. A lot of people have said that while continuing to maintain that basic style, which is certainly evident, that some things rubbed off. Was this an unconscious thing, if it occurred at all?

Well, unconscious, of course, but I hope it did rub off something. When Parker came along, it was a little late for me to try to be a Parker clone, and I was not prepared to put in the hours of practice that that kind of playing really requires. Well, not only that, I had no desire to sound like Parker, you know. I had my own thing, no matter how, you know, old-fashioned it may seem to some people. But that was me, and that’s all I was concerned with. But I certainly enjoy listening to Parker, and I say again I marvel at the things he did.
Getting back to this John Coltrane I won’t call it debate but the discussion you had, why was what he did, in your mind, at least, not as significant as what Charlie Parker was doing?
You mean to me or to others?
To you.
I don’t know. I just found Parker more interesting. That’s all, you know, but Coltrane had his thing, which just didn’t appeal to me that much. But I think to me Parker was more creative, much more.

Just going a step further, you were once given a blindfold test by Leonard Feather, and he played you some Ornette Coleman, which was yet another development maybe beyond Coltrane on the continuum, I guess. Your reaction was not favorable at all. It was one of the strongest reactions I’ve seen in print from you. Was there nothing in that period or that type of music that you found, personally, anything worthwhile in?
On that particular blindfold test, I think he also played something of Phil Woods’.
Right.
And Phil Woods and what’s his name, Coleman?
Ornette.
Ornette Coleman, that’s what you’d call unfair competition. So I shall go no further with that.
Okay. I’ll continue here with a little digression again. Someone just brought up the I guess we could call it an oxymoron, maybe, of rap music.

What, what? [Berger laughs.] I wouldn’t expect you to say that. There’s no such thing, as far as I’m concerned, as rap music. There is rap, and much of it is quite good, you know. But I’ve yet to hear one with any music to it. The beat, rhythm is there. I think that’s what’s very, very attractive to the kids. But rap music, as you say, that is an oxymoron.

As we draw to the end of this six-hour marathon, and just celebrating your eighty- fifth birthday, this may be a nice time to reflect on just some general, universal questions. Do you ever think about your place in—quote, unquote—the history of music and something like that? When people look at the history of music, is there something that you’d like to be remembered for more than anything else of all the things you’ve done?

No, all I would like to remember for is having been here. Whatever contribution I may have made, if any, is to be made by others, not by me . . . to be recognized by others, not by me. I don’t know that I’ve made any real contribution. I’ve done what I set out to do, and that was have fun with the music, enjoy it and perform it and listen to it, to other people. I must admit that I have, to my satisfaction, achieved much that I had not even thought of. Of course, there’s much left that I would like to do, but just what, I’m not sure. But I would just like to continue what I’m doing, you know, until the next eighty-five years.
Well, we’re already planning the hundredth celebration, so . . .
Well, that’s just around the corner.
That’s nothing.
Yeah, that’s nothing.
You mention that you’re satisfied with what you’ve done. Would you have changed anything specifically in retrospect?
Oh yes, I would have. I won’t say what, because there were opportunities I had that I think I goofed, and I can’t blame anybody else for.
What aspect of music did you enjoy the least?
Rap. [laughter]
Of things that you actually were forced to do, engaged in and . . .
Oh, things I was involved in? I don’t know. I enjoyed it all, you know. I can’t point any particular high spots. I just enjoyed it all.

Is there anyone that you would have . . . I mean, you played with virtually everyone in so many fields of music, but was there anyone that just comes to mind offhand that you would like to have worked with that you never had the opportunity to?
Not that I can recall at the moment.

As far as the future goes, you’re still planning tours. You’re still planning recordings. Are there any particular things you’d like to accomplish or particular projects that you would want to work on?

Nothing I can think of. Well, I’m playing next weekend with Claude Terry [phonetic] in France and I’m looking forward to playing with Dizzy on his October cruise. And there are others, I mean, that I hope to play with again before I play with Gabriel. But no, I don’t have any . . . nothing outstanding.
You still enjoy, obviously . . .
Oh, indeed.
. . . touring.
Yeah. Well, I don’t enjoy the touring. I enjoy being there and performing, but the touring itself, which is getting there and preparing to get there, no, I don’t enjoy that anymore.

How about the . . . I know you don’t like to single out younger musicians that have appeal to you, or you don’t want to slight anybody. But, in general, the music that you helped to create, nurture, shape, and get to the point that it is today, are you confident about its future?

Oh yes. Yes. I mean, not only its future, but its present. There are a lot of good things going on, a lot of things that I enjoy, and many young players that I think are really on the way somewhere, but not only that, they’ve really arrived. I won’t go into names, but there are many. So, in other words, I feel that the music itself is in good hands.
Okay. Is there anything you’d like to add or any message to people that may be using this interview in years to come or any small piece of advice y you would impart?

Well, all I would say is, to the budding musician or the instrumentalist, is try to find your own voice with respect to everybody that has gone before you or everybody who is here now. But try to find your own voice and say your own thing.
Okay. Well, you’ve certainly said yours very well. Thank you.
[End of interview]

segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview with Benny Carter
segments.summary: Ed Berger states the date, place and purpose of the interview and starts at the beginning.

segments.title: Born in the Bronx, San Juan Hill, expelled from school
segments.summary: Carter gives his birth, his father's jobs, the move to San Juan Hill, and being expelled from PS 141 at fourteen after a fight.

segments.title: Parents' names, ancestry and the family's musical members
segments.summary: He names his parents, says they were children of slaves with little ancestry known, and describes the musical relatives, including his cousin Cuban Bennett and the pawn shop saxophone.

segments.title: Meeting cousin Cuban Bennett in McDonald, Pennsylvania
segments.summary: Carter was sent to McDonald, PA at eleven, where he heard Cuban Bennett's lyrical trumpet, which he wanted to sound like.

segments.title: Cuban Bennett's career, style and death
segments.summary: Discussion of Cuban's New York career in the mid-twenties, his never recording, how Carter would liken his style to Clifford Brown, and uncertainty over when he died.

segments.title: Playing with Cuban Bennett in Earl Hines's Pittsburgh sextet
segments.summary: Carter played baritone with Cuban in Earl Hines's sextet in 1925 and describes him as easygoing and quietly funny.

segments.title: Out of school, the trumpet returned, a C melody saxophone from Harold Proctor
segments.summary: After leaving school he returned the trumpet he had bought, took a C melody saxophone and a few lessons from neighbor Harold Proctor.

segments.title: First gigs: Rex Stewart's matinee and Willy the Lion Smith's trio
segments.summary: He gets a dollar-and-a-quarter matinee on Rex Stewart's recommendation, then joins Willie the Lion Smith's trio and is told to get an alto, which his parents buy.

segments.title: First music he remembers: a combo across the street
segments.summary: The earliest music that impressed him was a neighborhood combo rehearsing with Bubber Miley and others.

segments.title: Parents' views of jazz and the saxophone
segments.summary: His churchgoing parents considered jazz the devil's music and wanted him to be a violinist or theologian.

segments.title: Early teachers: Proctor, Eugene Michaels, Rudy Powell and Arthur Reeves
segments.summary: He names his teachers and says Arthur Reeves shaped his sound, and mentions the Vereecken saxophone method.

segments.title: San Juan Hill neighbors: Bubber Miley, Procope, Bobby Stark, Roger Ramirez
segments.summary: Carter places his early studies in 1923-24 and names musicians who grew up near him.

segments.title: Dime-a-dance trio jobs with Freddy Johnson and Walter Johnson
segments.summary: Dance hall trios without bass, playing melody for dancers one or two choruses at a time.

segments.title: Sitting in at Leroy's in Harlem with Bill Basie
segments.summary: He went to Harlem to sit in and Bill Basie was kind to him at Leroy's; they discuss Basie's early stride style.

segments.title: Fats Waller and the song Nobody Knows
segments.summary: Carter met Waller in the late twenties, recorded with him with McKinney's, and finished Waller's song with lyricist Bud Allen.

segments.title: Legendary stride pianists who never recorded: Sam Weber, Seminole, Putney Dandridge
segments.summary: Carter recalls obscure Harlem stride pianists and doubts that Duke Ellington took part in that circle.

segments.title: Lessons from Willie the Lion Smith about playing in all keys
segments.summary: Smith, brusque but warm, made Carter stop pulling out his mouthpiece to play in the alto's awkward keys.

segments.title: Shot-up spaghetti joint in Brooklyn and gangsters in the music business
segments.summary: A mob shooting at a Brooklyn club, and what Carter knew of mobsters at Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club.

segments.title: Charlie Johnson's orchestra at Smalls' Paradise
segments.summary: Carter names the Harlem bands he played with, including June Clark's sextet and Charlie Johnson at Smalls' Paradise.

segments.title: Billy Paige's Broadway Syncopators and going to Pittsburgh
segments.summary: He joined Billy Paige's band at a Lenox Avenue club and went with them to Pittsburgh with his parents' consent.

segments.title: Horace Henderson and the Wilberforce Collegians; elected leader
segments.summary: Horace invited him to join the Wilberforce band; touring, the Club Bamville job, and the band electing Carter leader.

segments.title: Straightening out the Wilberforce and Charlie Johnson chronology
segments.summary: Berger and Carter reconstruct the order of his two Wilberforce periods and his time with Charlie Johnson.

segments.title: Battle of the bands with McKinney's Cotton Pickers at the Graystone
segments.summary: Carter's band beat McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit and he still has the trophy cup.

segments.title: First recordings with Charlie Johnson in 1928
segments.summary: Berger reminds him of his first documented recordings, two arrangements among four tunes.

segments.title: Teaching himself to arrange from stock arrangements
segments.summary: Carter spread stock arrangements out on the floor to study them part by part and soon wrote full arrangements.

segments.title: Substituting for Don Redman in Fletcher Henderson's band
segments.summary: He subbed for Redman for a week or two, and recalls not being able to hear downtown bands while white musicians could come up to Harlem.

segments.title: The Battle of the Century at Roseland: Henderson against Goldkette
segments.summary: The Goldkette band opposed Henderson during Carter's stint, and he recalls Bill Challis's arrangements.

segments.title: Frank Trumbauer as the inspiration to play saxophone
segments.summary: Hearing Trumbauer's records made him want to play the saxophone and he copied his solos.

segments.title: Other saxophonists: Wayne King, Rudy Wiedoft, Leonard Fields
segments.summary: Carter discusses saxophonists whose sound or technique impressed him.

segments.title: White musicians sitting in uptown without reciprocity
segments.summary: Jimmy Dorsey and Jack Teagarden came to Harlem, and Carter explains there was no animosity as it was the tenor of the times.

segments.title: Getting the Ellington job in 1926; hearing Bechet at the Kentucky Club
segments.summary: Duke asked Carter to fill in on saxophone; Carter recalls having heard the band with Bubber Miley and Sidney Bechet at the Kentucky Club.

segments.title: Standing of the Ellington band and the Richmond Club engagement
segments.summary: Musicians looked up more to Henderson's band; Carter recalls mostly Ellington's own music at a club on 57th Street.

segments.title: Becoming a regular in Fletcher Henderson's band, 1930
segments.summary: Carter's earlier recordings and arranging for Henderson, PDQ Blues, and the informal understanding that he would arrange after Redman left.

segments.title: Henderson's other arrangers: Charlie Dixon, Macomber, Glover, Nesbitt
segments.summary: Berger and Carter list the men who arranged for Henderson before and alongside Redman and Carter.

segments.title: Did arrangers compare notes? Fletcher and Horace Henderson as writers
segments.summary: Carter recalls no exchange with Redman or others, and says Fletcher's arranging was brought out later by Benny Goodman.

segments.title: How swing arranging developed and how Carter wrote
segments.summary: Asked about the rapid development of arrangement and placing soloists, Carter says he simply sat and wrote with a pencil, and talk turns to computer copying.

segments.title: Relation between his saxophone playing and his writing
segments.summary: Carter says improvised-style saxophone lines kind of dictate the sax section writing, and that nothing too complex or fast.

segments.title: Joining Chick Webb's orchestra and Webb's drumming
segments.summary: Carter says Webb had an uncanny eye for musicians and a style of his own.

segments.title: Arranging for Chick Webb, including Liza
segments.summary: He took arrangements in hoping they would be played; he does not recall whether Webb asked for Liza.

segments.title: Pianist Gabby Rogers with the Savoy engagement of 1928
segments.summary: After Horace left, the Collegians took Detroit pianist Gabby Rogers to the Savoy Ballroom.

segments.title: The Savoy Ballroom in 1928: the hall, the Savoy Sultans and the dancing crowd
segments.summary: Carter describes the Savoy's two bandstands, hostesses, the opposing bands, the book of the Savoy Playboys and the audiences.

segments.title: Becoming musical director of McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.summary: Bill McKinney invited him to Detroit as musical director; Roscoe Simmons fronted the band.

segments.title: The McKinney's book and its style
segments.summary: Carter says the band already had a large book and he doesn't know how much he added; Berger finds the recordings nostalgic.

segments.title: Taking up the trumpet again through Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: Cheatham encouraged him, handing over his own horn, at the Empire Ballroom in 1932.

segments.title: Forming his first orchestra in 1932
segments.summary: Carter recalls the first idea of leading a band, a rehearsal band and the early Empire Ballroom job, with Teddy Wilson coming later.

segments.title: Personnel of the 1932 band in the Boston revue
segments.summary: Berger reads out the first confirmed personnel from the Cocktails of 1932 review in Boston.

segments.title: Sorting out the chronology of the 1932-33 band and Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: Berger and Carter work out that the Empire Ballroom was 1933, that the rehearsal band came earlier, and when Carter took up the trumpet.

segments.title: Opening at the Empire Ballroom opposite Paul Whiteman
segments.summary: Carter tries to place the ballroom and recalls Whiteman's large dance orchestra on the other stand.

segments.title: John Hammond appears; the band never becomes solvent
segments.summary: Carter showed Hammond around Harlem; the band looked promising but never solvent; the first day ends before Teddy Wilson.

segments.title: Second day: self-education, reading and libraries
segments.summary: Berger opens the second day, August 7, 1992, and asks about Carter's informal education and reading.

segments.title: Writing poetry and lyrics, mostly for his wife Hilma
segments.summary: Carter has written little poetry and song words, mostly for his wife, but no prose.

segments.title: Sitting in, jam sessions and cutting contests
segments.summary: Musicians were kind to him, especially Basie; he was in many cutting sessions but recalls none by name.

segments.title: The 1933 band's first gigs and the Scottsboro benefit
segments.summary: The rehearsal band finds paying work and plays a benefit for the Scottsboro Boys with John Hammond.

segments.title: Hearing Teddy Wilson in Woonsocket; Hammond's role in the rehearsal band
segments.summary: Carter first heard Wilson with a band while with Henderson, and says John Hammond put no money into his band.

segments.title: Driving to Chicago to persuade Teddy Wilson to come to New York
segments.summary: Hammond financed the trip, Carter drove with George Rich, and they talked a shy Wilson into coming.

segments.title: What set Teddy Wilson's playing apart
segments.summary: Carter says Wilson was the closest thing to Art Tatum, with taste, technique and harmonic sensitivity.

segments.title: Teddy Wilson's first record date with Carter, the Chocolate Dandies
segments.summary: Within a day or two of his return, the group recorded Once Upon a Time and others.

segments.title: First recordings of the band in March 1933, with Carter vocals
segments.summary: Carter dislikes talk of his early vocals, and says recording was another gig that brought a check.

segments.title: Recording with Spike Hughes
segments.summary: Carter discusses Hughes's music and the claim that Carter influenced his writing.

segments.title: The October 1933 sessions: Lonesome Nights, Symphony in Riffs and Devil's Holiday
segments.summary: Carter recalls little about the integrated small-group date and the big band session and offers reasons he took no solos.

segments.title: Rehearsing the October 1933 pieces and the expanded saxophone section
segments.summary: Carter says musicians are better today, that they rehearsed first, and that the section grew from three to four saxes.

segments.title: Recordings with Mezz Mezzrow, Charlie Barnet and Bud Freeman
segments.summary: Berger runs through Carter's 1933-34 sideman sessions; Carter has forgotten several, including the Bud Freeman date with Willie the Lion and Chick Webb.

segments.title: Integrated recording groups felt natural
segments.summary: Carter says he never thought of mixed-race sessions as unusual.

segments.title: Opening the big band policy at the Apollo Theater, January 1934
segments.summary: Carter's band played two weeks at the Apollo with Ralph Cooper as master of ceremonies, before the show format was set.

segments.title: Choosing I May Be Wrong as his theme song
segments.summary: The theme was picked casually for the Apollo and stuck for fifty years.

segments.title: Commercial success versus artistic integrity in his bands
segments.summary: Carter says he did not think in those terms, though he sometimes used other arrangers hoping for commercial results.

segments.title: Gunther Schuller on Carter's talent being too diverse for the public
segments.summary: Berger reads Schuller's explanation of Carter's commercial failure; Carter thinks it is largely right.

segments.title: Schuller on missing identity and Ellington's patience
segments.summary: More of Schuller's criticism; Carter agrees his orchestras lacked an identifiable identity and does not compare himself to Ellington.

segments.title: A Down Beat blindfold test and Charlie Parker's influence
segments.summary: Carter respects the honesty of a critic's remark about one of his records; they defer the Parker discussion.

segments.title: Were jazz musicians artists before bebop?
segments.summary: Carter says he always saw himself as a musician and never thought of the artist or entertainer distinction.

segments.title: Art versus commerce and serious music
segments.summary: Carter says art and commercial success can coexist and jokes about the green muse.

segments.title: Symphony in Riffs, once for dancing, now analyzed as concert art
segments.summary: Carter finds it gratifying but leaves the analysis to Schuller and Marsalis.

segments.title: Irving Mills as Carter's first publisher
segments.summary: Mills heard Carter's riff, which became Blues in My Heart, and published his music; Carter praises Mills's role with Ellington.

segments.title: Names added to songs: publishers, bandleaders and Edgar Sampson's tunes
segments.summary: Carter discusses taking composer credit, and says Edgar Sampson wrote Stompin' at the Savoy while Goodman's name went on.

segments.title: The 1933 orchestra dries up in 1934
segments.summary: Carter was working to pay rent, not to hold the band together.

segments.title: Arranging for Benny Goodman's first big band and the Let's Dance broadcasts
segments.summary: Carter arranged for Goodman at the Billy Rose Music Hall, perhaps before Fletcher Henderson did.

segments.title: Joining Willie Bryant's band as a trumpet-playing sideman
segments.summary: After his band broke up he took a job, mainly on trumpet, with Willie Bryant, who was not a musician.

segments.title: The telegram offer from Willie Lewis in Paris
segments.summary: Carter received a telegram from Willie Lewis in 1935 offering him a job in Paris.

segments.title: Why he went to Europe, and the word expatriate
segments.summary: Carter says he wanted to see another culture, went for almost three years, and meant to return only for a visit.

segments.title: Playing society dance music with Willie Lewis at Chez Florence
segments.summary: The Lewis band played show tunes and melody for a jet-set crowd, with few Carter arrangements.

segments.title: Meeting Django Reinhardt in Paris
segments.summary: Carter found Django quiet and shy and describes his playing as a revelation despite his injured hand.

segments.title: Leonard Feather and arranging for the BBC in London
segments.summary: Feather cabled him to write for the BBC radio staff band; he wrote about three arrangements a week and could not get a permit to play.

segments.title: Treatment in Europe and the Hippodrome concert
segments.summary: Carter was received with respect, and his one permitted public playing was a concert at the Hippodrome.

segments.title: Leonard Feather's recordings and Waltzing the Blues
segments.summary: Feather produced everything Carter recorded there; Waltzing the Blues was Feather's idea and unwritten.

segments.title: Work permit limits and the Royal Academy of Music
segments.summary: Having to leave England every three months stopped Carter from starting formal study at the Academy.

segments.title: Rosamond Johnson's help with his first film work
segments.summary: Rosamond Johnson in London helped him as he prepared a British film score.

segments.title: The European musicians and the Scheveningen international band
segments.summary: Carter names the players in his European units and says the interracial, international band was about getting the best players.

segments.title: The 1937 Paris saxophone session with Hawkins, Combelle and Ekyan
segments.summary: Carter fondly remembers Alix Combelle and Andre Ekyan, who recorded with him and Coleman Hawkins.

segments.title: Charles Delaunay's account of Carter sketching the arrangements in the studio
segments.summary: Delaunay says Carter wrote the ensembles on the spot for Honeysuckle Rose and Crazy Rhythm; the last two numbers were a jam.

segments.title: News of American swing reaching Europe
segments.summary: Carter heard records and knew of Goodman's success, but felt little had developed in the meantime.

segments.title: Coleman Hawkins as a man and player, and the rivalry that was not
segments.summary: Carter sat beside Hawkins in Henderson's band, found him private and likeable, and sees no rivalry in Europe.

segments.title: Deciding to come home from Europe
segments.summary: There was no big reason, he simply wanted to go home for a while.

segments.title: Sid Catlett's drumming
segments.summary: Interview resumes on Carter's eighty-fifth birthday; he praises Catlett as a gentle giant and wishes today's drummers had heard him.

segments.title: What he looks for in drummers and his view of drum solos
segments.summary: Carter wants a drummer who makes the one clear and prefers short drum solos, though audiences love them.

segments.title: Chu Berry in the 1932-33 band
segments.summary: Carter says he found musicians by being on the scene, and describes Chu Berry as like Hawkins but with his own voice.

segments.title: Hearing Lester Young on alto in St. Paul
segments.summary: He heard Young on alto, playing more notes in a Parker-like way, while with McKinney's.

segments.title: Roy Eldridge in Pittsburgh in 1925
segments.summary: Carter played once or twice with Roy and Joe Eldridge's Pittsburgh band and admired Roy's originality.

segments.title: Art Tatum in Detroit in 1928 and the 1954 session
segments.summary: Carter heard Tatum in 1928 and was amazed; he recorded with him in 1954 and found accompanying him easy.

segments.title: Soloing on several instruments in the European recordings
segments.summary: Carter says the multi-instrument records were suggested by producers like Feather, and that he may have been showing off a bit.

segments.title: Learning the trumpet with Doc Cheatham's help
segments.summary: Carter practiced on his own with Cheatham as the only teacher and bought a Conn 22B on his advice.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's influence through records
segments.summary: Carter knew Armstrong only through records and does not recall copying his solos.

segments.title: Playing the clarinet as a doubling instrument
segments.summary: He picked up clarinet as a dance-band double, probably with Charlie Johnson, and let it taper off in the mid-forties.

segments.title: Playing lead alto and Marshall Royal as his standard
segments.summary: Carter has no tips for lead players, says a lead should have authority, and holds up Marshall Royal.

segments.title: Why the trumpet is his favorite instrument
segments.summary: He says the lead trumpet leads the whole orchestra, and he hears songs like Body and Soul on trumpet.

segments.title: Other instruments he has played or bought
segments.summary: Carter has no instrument he wishes he had learned; he bought a violin only to learn about it for writing.

segments.title: Returning to the United States in 1938 and the state of the band scene
segments.summary: He intended to form a big band and found the scene little changed, with Goodman the hot name.

segments.title: A more commercial approach and the break with Decca
segments.summary: Carter says he tried for more commercial appeal and a Decca session of novelty songs led him to move to Bluebird.

segments.title: The big band shrinks to a sextet in 1941
segments.summary: Lack of work ended the orchestra; the sextet at Kelly's Stables had Gillespie, Kenny Clarke and others.

segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie in the sextet
segments.summary: Carter says Gillespie was far advanced and that the sextet used small arrangements, originals and pop tunes, none recorded.

segments.title: Management pressure to fire Dizzy at the Famous Door
segments.summary: Carter ignored club owner Irving Alexander's dislike of Gillespie's music and kept him on.

segments.title: First trip to the West Coast and the Swing Club in Hollywood
segments.summary: The reformed big band toured west in 1942 and played Billy Berg's Swing Club, briefly with Buddy Rich.

segments.title: Armed forces broadcasts and the wartime band's changing personnel
segments.summary: He was asked to do forces broadcasts and record for Capitol; the draft took players and younger modernists came in.

segments.title: J. J. Johnson, Max Roach and Miles Davis join the band
segments.summary: Carter recalls younger players, with Miles joining in St. Louis for a few weeks in 1946.

segments.title: Miles Davis as a young man and the Grammy request
segments.summary: Carter found Miles quiet and lyrical, let him stay in his house, and later accepted a Grammy for him.

segments.title: Eighteen-year-old J. J. Johnson and his parents' consent
segments.summary: Johnson's parents vetted Carter before letting him go to California, like Carter's own mother had.

segments.title: J. J. Johnson's personality and his arrangements for the band
segments.summary: Carter found him outgoing and well educated, and his charts were already played on forces broadcasts.

segments.title: Max Roach in the big band
segments.summary: Roach's innovative drumming made it hard to find the one, and the band had to sneak back in after his solos.

segments.title: Day four: why he settled in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Carter chose Los Angeles for its weather, pace and studio work, though he never intended to stay.

segments.title: Wartime travel on the road to California
segments.summary: The band travelled mostly by train, then played two weeks at the Rendezvous in Salt Lake City.

segments.title: The Los Angeles jazz scene and ballrooms in the early forties
segments.summary: Carter recalls the Swing Club, Streets of Paris with Art Tatum, Central Avenue, the Palladium and Casa Manana.

segments.title: Integrated band with Buddy Rich, Art Pepper and Joe Albany
segments.summary: Carter says he had no difficulty with white players, tells of the St. Louis dancers asking about his pianist, and discusses Art Pepper's book.

segments.title: Getting into film work through Stormy Weather
segments.summary: Mike Gould recommended him to Irving Mills; the pay beat the band, and he disbanded in 1946.

segments.title: Writing for film: timing, catching action and directors
segments.summary: Carter says cues must fit exact timings; he found directors' direction helpful rather than constraining.

segments.title: Black composers in the Hollywood studios before him
segments.summary: Carter names Phil Moore, Will Vodery and Lee Young and disclaims being a barrier-breaker.

segments.title: Renting a house in Hollywood with help from Mike Gould
segments.summary: Gould found him a rented house on Vista Street.

segments.title: Buying a house and the neighborhood suit
segments.summary: After house-hunting runs into the usual excuses, Carter won a lawsuit from a development association but moved anyway, and later bought in Gould's name.

segments.title: Restrictive covenants and his neighbors
segments.summary: Carter stalled until covenants fell, a saxophone teacher tried to organize a petition, and neighbors were friendly.

segments.title: Merging the black and white musicians' union locals in 1953
segments.summary: Carter circulated petitions with Buddy Collette and Alfred Newman signing first and the two locals voted to amalgamate.

segments.title: Opposition to the union merger
segments.summary: Carter thinks the opposition from the black local came mostly from its officers.

segments.title: Was he stereotyped as a jazz writer in the studios?
segments.summary: He says no more than a white jazz writer would be.

segments.title: Advice from film composers, teaching himself, and the broadening effect of film
segments.summary: He exchanged ideas with other film composers and says film work broadened him.

segments.title: Television writing and deadlines
segments.summary: There was little difference from film except deadlines, which he found stressful but motivating.

segments.title: Composing away from the piano
segments.summary: Carter calls the piano a crutch and works at the kitchen table.

segments.title: Frank Comstock's arrangements, including Poinciana
segments.summary: Carter bought outside arrangements for his band; Comstock arranged Poinciana, which people took for his own.

segments.title: How work was handed out in Hollywood
segments.summary: Carter disagrees that work isn't commensurate with talent among studio players, and mentions rejected film scores.

segments.title: Films he was proud of and ideas for later
segments.summary: He says it was all a gig and keeps stray ideas on separate paper.

segments.title: Background music and reusing film melodies
segments.summary: Music should be felt and not heard; unlike Mancini he has no songs that came from film scores.

segments.title: Ghost writing, orchestrating and film credits
segments.summary: Carter says he was never ghost-written for, though in film he mostly developed another composer's themes as orchestrator.

segments.title: Playing less in the fifties and sixties
segments.summary: Carter went along with whatever was in demand and did not worry about playing more.

segments.title: The Los Angeles jazz concert hall on Crenshaw
segments.summary: Carter and agent Jack Hampton opened a jazz theater for young people, which failed within weeks for lack of capital.

segments.title: Why film scoring changed and synthesizers
segments.summary: Carter blames changing tastes and self-contained groups for the end of the great film composers and says he used a synthesizer early.

segments.title: Whether he played C melody saxophone on The Snows of Kilimanjaro
segments.summary: Berger says he played C melody on the 1957 soundtrack; Carter does not remember it.

segments.title: Returning to touring and playing in the 1970s
segments.summary: Film work dwindled after Stanley Wilson died, and offers of concerts and solo playing picked up.

segments.title: Morroe Berger brings him to Princeton and abroad
segments.summary: Berger invited him to Baldwin-Wallace, Princeton and Cornell and on a Mideast tour, and Ed Berger co-authored the 1982 book.

segments.title: Fourth tape: first time in a classroom
segments.summary: Carter says Morroe Berger put him at ease about having no degree or experience.

segments.title: Why he never took private students; the key he did not know he used
segments.summary: Carter lacked patience for beginners, and the instrument is so automatic that he can't say which keys he uses.

segments.title: His teaching approach: learning from students
segments.summary: He looks things up with students and asks their opinions of how to play, as at the Rutgers concerts.

segments.title: Asking students to play a melody
segments.summary: Carter wants to hear the soul in a melody rather than technical display.

segments.title: Practice habits and layoffs
segments.summary: He now practices only before performances, often playing along with a record.

segments.title: Coltrane transcriptions and Charlie Parker as the last innovation
segments.summary: Carter denies practicing with Coltrane solos and says Parker was the last true innovation for him.

segments.title: Meeting Charlie Parker and his effect on Carter's playing
segments.summary: Carter had a favorable impression of Parker and says he had no wish to be a Parker clone.

segments.title: Why Parker over Coltrane, and the Ornette Coleman blindfold test
segments.summary: Carter found Parker more creative, and jokes that Ornette against Phil Woods was unfair competition.

segments.title: Rap as an oxymoron
segments.summary: Carter says there is rap but no rap music, as the beat appeals to kids.

segments.title: His place in history, regrets and what he enjoyed
segments.summary: Carter wants only to be remembered as having been here, would change some missed opportunities, and enjoyed it all.

segments.title: Future plans, touring, and confidence in the music's future
segments.summary: He still plays and records but no longer enjoys travel; he feels jazz is in good hands.

segments.title: Advice to young musicians and close of the interview
segments.summary: Carter urges young players to find their own voice; Berger ends the interview.

segments.title: Back-of-book name index
segments.summary: The transcript's printed index of names and page numbers, not part of the conversation.
